The personal responsible for this proof is Laszlo Polgar. He was a man with an enthusiasm for chess, but no major successes. After extensive research on the topic he decided that any child ought be able to raised to be a 'genius' in most any subject, and wanted to carry out an experiment. As he was single he sought a wife who was similarly interested and found a woman, with no particular success in chess herself, to also partake in his experiment.

They had three daughters - Sofia, Judith, and Susan. From age 4 they were grilled in chess by two parents who while having no particular 'talent' for chess, were indeed skilled teachers a trait Laszlo specifically sought out in his wife. Sofia would become an international master. Susan and Judith grandmasters. Susan would become women's world champion and a grandmaster. Their ascent was really only stopped by them stepping away from their father and the board - getting married, and so on. Laszlo more or less proved that at least in chess, which is traditionally one of the most 'prodigy' oriented fields, it's all about training and work.

Whenever a character is created, they are set with hidden maximum scores for any of the skills available in game. We can't see what are maximum scores are on any given skill, but you will notice you gain skill points more quickly in things you have a higher maximum score for. This is because skill points are gained by percentage of maximum score. The designers did this so we could figure out what our characters are good at more quickly, instead of grinding away at some skill we won't ever get over a 50/264.

Let's say you have a maximum skill of 50 in painting. You grind it up to 50%, you are a 25. Someone else has a maximum score of 250. They take the time to grind the skill up to 10%. They have the same skill level as you, in 1/5 of the work.

Now, there are some guilds that will help you increase your maximum score, or make it easier to reach your maximum potential, but these take a lot of in game time, and cost a lot of currency.
